A Stack Implementation of a Shift-Reduce Parser
• There are four possible actions of a shift-Reduce parser: 
• Shift : The next input symbol is shifted onto the top of the stack. 
• Reduce: Replace the handle on the top of the stack by the non-terminal. 
• Accept: Successful completion of parsing. 
• Error: Parser discovers a syntax error, and calls an error recovery routine. 
• Initial stack just contains only the end-marker $. 
• The end of the input string is marked by the end-marker $
48
Think of the parser as repeatedly asking: “What should I do with the next input symbol?”
“This is the bottom of the stack.”
“There are no more input symbols.”

pages.source_path: data\raw\college\5. Bottom Up Parser Compiler Design-47-58.pdf
pages.text:
Shift reduce parsing … 
• Symbols on the left of “. or |” are kept on a stack 
 
– Top of the stack is at “. or |” 
 
– Shift pushes a terminal on the stack 
 
– Reduce pops symbols (RHS of production) and pushes a non terminal (LHS 
 
of production) onto the stack 
• The most important issue: when to shift and when to reduce 
• Reduce action should be taken only if the result can be reduced to the start symbol 
49
So, the fundamental cycle is:    SHIFT →SHIFT →REDUCE →SHIFT →REDUCE →⋯
Until:     $S$⇒ACCEPT

Issues in bottom-up parsing
• How do we know which action to take 
 
– whether to shift or reduce 
 
– which production to use for reduction? 
•  Sometimes parser can reduce but it should not:

pages.text:
Issues in bottom-up parsing
• Sometimes parser can reduce in different ways! 
• Given stack δ and input symbol a, should the parser 
 
– Shift a onto stack (making it δa) 
 
– Reduce by some production A → β assuming that stack has form αβ (making it αA) 
 
– Stack can have many combinations of αβ  
 
 
(But sometimes both seem possible at the same time, leading to confusion.)
 
– How to keep track of length of β?
• The issue in bottom-up parsing is that the parser doesn’t always know whether to shift more input or 
reduce immediately, and if reduce, then by which rule.
• LR parsers solve this using carefully constructed parse tables so that only one action is valid in each state.
51

Handles
• The basic steps of a bottom-up parser are 
• To identify a substring within a rightmost sentential form that matches the LHS of a rule. 
• When this substring is replaced by the LHS of the matching rule, it must produce the previous 
rightmost-sentential form. 
• Such a substring is called a handle (The substring that should be reduced next in a right-sentential form)
Identifying the correct handle at each step tells the parser: (1) what to reduce (find the Handle), (2) and by 
which production (the production who’s RHS is handle)

Handle (Definition in Simple Words: A handle is the part of the string that we can reduce next.)
• A handle of a string (right sentential form) γ is:
• a production rule A → β
• and an **occurrence of β inside γ`
• such that replacing β with A gives you the previous string in the rightmost 
derivation of γ.
• So, a handle is what you can reduce right now in bottom-up parsing.
Grammer:
E → E + T | T
T → id
Input:  id + id
Right Most Derivation
1. E
2. E + T
3. E + id 
4. id + id

Handle: Observation
• Is this scenario possible: 
• 𝛼𝛽𝛾 is the content of the stack 
• 𝐴 →𝛾 is a handle 
• The stack content reduces to 𝛼𝛽𝐴 
• Now B → 𝛽 is the handle 
56
Can a handle be buried inside the stack?
No. In a valid shift-reduce parse, the handle is always the portion at the top of the 
stack that can be reduced. If a non-terminal occurs above it, that lower portion 
cannot be the next handle.
